changes.old: ### Ширина поиска, пробные продолжения и цена оценки
changes.new: ### Creative writing: select a plan, then a passage The creative-writing task supplies four unrelated sentences. The output must contain four paragraphs, with each paragraph ending in its assigned sentence. Meeting those four local constraints does not ensure that the paragraphs form a coherent passage. In the example below, Plan 1 moves from a handstand to an astronaut, then to a conversation in a bar and finally to personal identity. Plan 2 connects the same material through an unusual self-help book. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/tot-reconciliation-2026-10-30/tot-creative-search.png]] *Shunyu Yao et al., [Tree of Thoughts, Figure 4, p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.10601v2#page=7), [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Complete original figure and English caption, cropped from the PDF without redrawing. Plan 2 receives three of the five votes; the other plans are discarded.* In [§4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.10601v2#S4.SS2), the authors use two generation-and-selection stages. First, they independently sample five plans from the planning prompt. A comparison prompt presents all five candidates together; five sampled responses each select a candidate after comparing the alternatives. The plan with the most votes survives. Next, the model samples five complete passages conditioned on that plan, and another five comparison responses select the final passage. The search has depth two and retains one state after each selection: five plans → one plan → five passages → one passage. It has one intermediate thought, the plan. It does not search separately over the four paragraphs, and it does not generate passages from all five plans. If the selected plan turns out to be unhelpful, this configuration does not revisit a rejected plan. This evaluator differs from the Game of 24 value prompt. A value prompt judges one partial solution against the task; the writing vote prompt compares a set of alternatives. Three votes for Plan 2 are a count of sampled preferences, not a calibrated probability that the plan will produce good writing. A candidate can win a plurality without receiving more than half the votes. All candidates and all judges still come from the same model. The pinned [TextTask](https://github.com/princeton-nlp/tree-of-thought-llm/blob/8050e67d0e3a0fddc424d7fa5801538722a4c4cc/src/tot/tasks/text.py) sets two stages, stopping the first at the passage delimiter. Its vote parser counts valid candidate indices; an unparseable vote contributes nothing. The shared greedy BFS selection keeps the first candidate on a tie. These parser and tie rules belong to that implementation, rather than to the general definition of ToT. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/tot-reconciliation-2026-10-30/tot-creative-results.png]] *Shunyu Yao et al., [Figure 5, p. 7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.10601v2#page=7), CC BY 4.0. Both original panels, all axis labels and the full caption. The right panel separates a ToT preference, a tie and a CoT preference.* Selection and final evaluation use different prompts. For the reported automatic evaluation, GPT-4 assigns each completed passage five scores from 1 to 10; the mean is the reported score. Across 100 inputs, the paper reports means of 6.19 for direct prompting, 6.93 for CoT and 7.56 for ToT. These are judgments of coherency, not percentages of correctly solved tasks. The human comparison, performed by a subset of the authors with passage order randomized and method identity hidden, preferred ToT in 41 pairs, CoT in 21 and found 38 similarly coherent. It was not an independent large-scale reader study. The same figure also reports iterative refinement. Refining a direct output raised its mean score to 7.67, while refining a ToT output raised it to 7.91. Thus these experiments do not establish that this tree search outperforms every other use of an additional inference budget. ### Mini Crosswords: constraints, pruning and backtracking A 5×5 crossword has ten clues: five horizontal and five vertical. A proposed word changes five cells, which also constrain five crossing words. After filling h1 with TASKS and h2 with MOTOR, the first vertical word has the pattern TM___. Adding SALON at h4 changes that pattern to TM_S_. The evaluator must decide whether a word matching both the pattern and the clue “To heap” remains plausible. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/tot-reconciliation-2026-10-30/tot-crossword-dfs.png]] *Shunyu Yao et al., [Tree of Thoughts, Figure 6, p. 8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.10601v2#page=8), CC BY 4.0. Complete original figure and English caption. The proposal queue orders candidate actions; the state evaluator rejects the SALON branch, and DFS returns to the parent before trying GRAND.* The generator proposes an action containing both a location and a word, such as h4. salon. It can propose different clues and several answers to one clue. The original proposal format also asks for a confidence label. Repeated proposals are combined by adding the weights of those labels; this produces the order in which DFS tries actions. In the pinned [notebook](https://github.com/princeton-nlp/tree-of-thought-llm/blob/8050e67d0e3a0fddc424d7fa5801538722a4c4cc/scripts/crosswords/search_crosswords-dfs.ipynb), the weights are certain = 1, high = 0.5, medium = 0.2 and low = 0.1. They are hand-chosen priorities, not probabilities. For example, SALON proposed once as certain, once as medium and once as low gets 1.3. GRAND proposed twice as high gets 1.0. SALON is therefore tried first. The following calculation uses explicit responses, not a model call. ```python import math def crossword_priorities(proposals): weights = {'certain': 1.0, 'high': 0.5, 'medium': 0.2, 'low': 0.1} scores = {} for action, label in proposals: scores[action] = scores.get(action, 0.0) + weights[label] return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True) def column_pattern(rows, column): return ''.join(row[column] for row in rows) proposals = [ ('h4. salon', 'certain'), ('h3. grand', 'high'), ('h4. salon', 'medium'), ('h3. grand', 'high'), ('h4. salon', 'low'), ] ordered = crossword_priorities(proposals) assert ordered[0][0] == 'h4. salon' assert math.isclose(ordered[0][1], 1.3) assert ordered[1] == ('h3. grand', 1.0) parent = ['TASKS', 'MOTOR', '_____', '_____', '_____'] child = parent.copy() child[3] = 'SALON' assert column_pattern(parent, 0) == 'TM___' assert column_pattern(child, 0) == 'TM_S_' assert parent[3] == '_____' # The saved parent is unchanged. print(ordered, column_pattern(child, 0)) ``` The second evaluator asks whether each constrained clue can still be filled. If it labels even one checked clue impossible, the search prunes that child's subtree. In Figure 6, TM_S_ receives that label. DFS then restores the board with TASKS and MOTOR, removes SALON from the action history, and tries the next action, h3. grand. GRAND is an alternative to explore, not a certified solution. Restoring only the text of the action history while keeping SALON's letters on the board would explore a different state. The released environment and the search controller have separate roles. [MiniCrosswordsEnv.step](https://github.com/princeton-nlp/tree-of-thought-llm/blob/8050e67d0e3a0fddc424d7fa5801538722a4c4cc/src/tot/tasks/crosswords.py) writes a proposed word and marks overwritten nonblank letters as changed. The DFS controller rejects a child with such a change and restores its saved board, status flags and step counter after exploring a candidate. The environment alone does not enforce the no-overwrite rule. There is also a boundary case in this notebook: when the child cap is exceeded, the loop breaks before its reset statement. At that exit, the current environment can retain the newly tried child's board. The caller normally restores its own saved state, but the root has no such caller. The visited-state log, rather than this leftover board, defines the paper's output selection. A new implementation should restore state even on an early exit, for example with a finally block. Its prompt-status routine skips patterns with fewer than two known letters; it can also evaluate filled words. It is not an exhaustive dictionary solver. There are reproducibility differences between the paper and the released notebook. Section 4.3 describes five proposal samples per state and at most ten intermediate steps. The pinned notebook requests eight proposal samples, continues only while the environment step is less than ten, and explores at most three admitted children per state. Its 100-step limit counts entries added to the search log, not network requests or generated tokens. Rejected candidates and the separate proposal/evaluation completions do not have a one-to-one relationship with that counter. The notebook restores state between siblings, so this budget is also different from the depth of a single path. The paper outputs the deepest visited state, choosing the first one on a tie. That is a usable rule when ground-truth answers are unavailable, but the deepest state need not contain the most correct letters. On 20 selected crosswords, the reported ToT output has 78% correct letters, 60% correct words and 20% completely solved games, which is four games. Choosing the best visited state with ground-truth access instead gives seven solved games. That oracle result diagnoses the output-selection rule; a deployed solver cannot select it without knowing the answers. Pruning can also discard a solution. The authors report that the evaluator sometimes rejects valid rare or obsolete words. Without pruning, the search visited correct solutions for four games, but its output rule returned only one of them; three of those visited solutions were not found by the pruned search within its budget. Backtracking, proposal quality, pruning and final selection therefore fail in different ways. The example above checks the priority and crossing-letter calculations; it does not reproduce GPT-4's crossword results. [Yao et al., §4.3 and Table 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.10601v2#S4.SS3). ### What the original comparisons measure The Game of 24 results use 100 games, indices 901–1,000 in the source's difficulty ordering. ToT with width one solves 45%, while width five solves 74%. The best-of-100 CoT oracle solves 49%, not less than the width-one result. This oracle selects a valid answer using correctness information; CoT self-consistency instead votes over the 100 answers and scores 9%. A method that generates a correct candidate and one that reliably selects it have different success rates. The published token costs also depend on the task. Appendix B.3 reports approximately 5.5k generated tokens per Game of 24 case for ToT, versus 6.7k for 100 CoT samples. Creative writing uses about 4k generated tokens for ToT versus 0.9k for one CoT response. The comparison is neither a universal “100 calls” rule nor a present-day latency measurement. The model, prompts, candidate lengths, evaluator, caching and stopping conditions determine the cost. [Yao et al., Table 2 and Appendix B.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.10601v2#page=14). For search that includes actions and observations from an external environment, continue with [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/17 Tools и Agents/67 Память, планирование и оркестрация агентов#LATS: дерево с наблюдениями среды|LATS and agent planning]]. A copied crossword board can be restored locally; an external action requires its own rollback or simulation semantics. ### Ширина поиска, пробные продолжения и цена оценки
